The hadronic amplitude from the DPM model is combined with the Coulomb amplitude to form the full elastic differential cross section model, which is fitted to the measured angular distribution in the LuminosityFit framework to extract the absolute luminosity while preventing unphysical mathematical fluctuations across beam momentum scans. [evidence.9b25e3c227798bc426619240, evidence.09e1e56c03a9c1741b55b69c, evidence.4bfb7160f3c8158ba59d70f2]
Employing the DPM parameterization also ensures that the theoretical fit model in LuminosityFit is identical to the PANDA official DPM event generator, maintaining model consistency between simulated data and luminosity extraction for systematic uncertainty studies. claims.claim_text: The theoretical purpose of the Dual Parton Model (DPM) in high-energy antiproton-proton elastic scattering is to provide a robust phenomenological description of the hadronic amplitude across a wide range of momentum transfers (|t|), capturing diffractive structures such as dips and secondary maxima that simple exponential parameterizations fail to describe.

The hadronic amplitude from the DPM model is combined with the Coulomb amplitude to form the full elastic differential cross section model, which is fitted to the measured angular distribution in the LuminosityFit framework to extract the absolute luminosity while preventing unphysical mathematical fluctuations across beam momentum scans.

Employing the DPM parameterization also ensures that the theoretical fit model in LuminosityFit is identical to the PANDA official DPM event generator, maintaining model consistency between simulated data and luminosity extraction for systematic uncertainty studies.

LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION - THE LUMINOSITY FIT FRAMEWORK
This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. One possibility is to correct the measured data for the effects introduced by the ¯ PANDA spectrometer, which then allows a direct comparison with the pure elastic scattering model. Alternatively, the pure model can be modified to include all of the effects that arise during the measurement, so that is directly comparable with the data. The first option is in practice not feasible as required operations such as deconvolutions, which undo the detector resolution of the data, require very large amounts of data and a constant resolution to work reliably. On these grounds the second option was chosen, allowing for far more flexibility, extraction power and precision. The construction of the fit model with all of the transformations and correction procedures of the elastic scattering cross section is presented in detail in the following. Results on the extracted luminosity precision and studies of systematic uncertainties are presented in the next chapter.

To overcome the severe limitations of simple analytical parameterizations, the Dual Parton Model (DPM) is employed as a robust phenomenological framework to describe high-energy ¯ 𝑝𝑝 elastic scattering [124, 125]. For the specific purpose of luminosity determination at PANDA, the primary practical advantage of the DPM lies in its ability to accurately model the hadronic amplitude across a wide range of momentum transfers ( | 𝑡 | ) without relying on unstable free parameters. Simple exponential parameterizations of the hadronic amplitude (e.g., 𝑒 -𝑏 | 𝑡 | ) via Eq. 3.6 are valid only at small momentum transfers [126, 127]. They completely fail to describe the complex diffractive structures, such as pronounced dips and secondary maxima, that inherently appear at larger | 𝑡 | values in ¯ 𝑝𝑝 scattering. Furthermore, attempting to extract the luminosity by treating fundamental variables like 𝜎 𝑡𝑜𝑡 , 𝑏 , and 𝜌 as independent free parameters for every single energy scan point can easily lead to unphysical mathematical fluctuations in the fit results. To overcome these experimental and phenomenological limitations, a more complicated DPM-based model is employed [128]:

3.4 Track Reconstruction and Event Preparation
The raw data acquired by the Luminosity Detector consists of digitized pixel hits distributed across four detector planes. To perform a precision luminosity analysis, these discrete electronic signals must be transformed into physical particle trajectories and, crucially, propagated back to the interaction point (IP) through the complex magnetic field to determine the scattering angles. The reconstruction chain is fully implemented within the PandaRoot framework as discussed before. The procedure consists of four sequential stages: Digitization and Hit Reconstruction, Track Finding, Track Fitting, Track Filtering and Back-Propagation, as illustrated in Figure 3.5.

The LMD detects antiprotons scattered at very small angles (3 -9 mrad). Using Eqs. 3.9 and 3.10, the corresponding momentum transfer | 𝑡 | can be calculated, as shown in Figure 3.3. Unfortunately, | 𝑡 | is not always at very small values where the Coulomb term dominates. At the beam momentum of 3 . 5 GeV /𝑐 , the hadronic term begins to take great effects, while at 12 GeV /𝑐 , the hadronic term dominates. Therefore, the full expression of Eq. 3.8 must be used to fit the measured differential cross section to extract the luminosity.

With these much simpler transformations, occurring especially frequently in the convolution algorithms needed for the beam divergence smearing and detector resolution smearing, the computation times of the luminosity fit are reduced dramatically 2 . Now the coordinate system rotation Jacobi determinant is relatively simple and can be calculated analytically as
In addition the periodicity in φ is removed also making some algorithms simpler. Finally the visualization of the results is more intuitive and easier to understand. In the following an example will be worked out to clarify the actual divergence smearing con- volution algorithm. It works on a two dimensional grid and has two input models 3 and outputs a smeared model. In the example the signal function that will undergo the effect of divergence smearing is a uniform function defined in the range from -2 . 0 mrad to 2 . 0 mrad in both dimensions θ x and θ y . For the divergence model a normalized 2 D gaussian function is used. These are depicted in figure 28 . The algorithm now discretizes both models on a specified grid, concretely in this example 14 chunks on each dimension. The divergence model grid is adjusted so that the grid constant is equivalent to the one of the signal model. Now for each 2 D bin in the signal model space, an integral of its content is performed and distributed to the neighboring bins according to the integral values of the divergence model bins. The integrals are evaluated with MC integration. Pictorially speaking the divergence model center is placed on top of each signal model bin, so that the bin boundaries match, and the previously mentioned content distribution is performed. The divergence smeared result can be seen in figure 28 .

implemented as a generator in the PANDAroot framework yet. Nevertheless, as shown
by results of in the following, it is more accurate and most probably will be used for the

claims.claim_text: The theoretical purpose of the Dual Parton Model (DPM) in high-energy antiproton-proton elastic scattering is to provide a robust phenomenological description of the hadronic amplitude across a wide range of momentum transfers (|t|), capturing diffractive structures such as dips and secondary maxima that simple exponential parameterizations fail to describe.

The hadronic amplitude from the DPM model is combined with the Coulomb amplitude to form the full elastic differential cross section model, which is fitted to the measured angular distribution in the LuminosityFit framework to extract the absolute luminosity while preventing unphysical mathematical fluctuations across beam momentum scans.

Employing the DPM parameterization also ensures that the theoretical fit model in LuminosityFit is identical to the PANDA official DPM event generator, maintaining model consistency between simulated data and luminosity extraction for systematic uncertainty studies.

### 3.3 First PID pass and POCA determination

The first PID pass is implemented by:

- `macro/target/pid_complete.C`

It configures `PndPidCorrelator` with:

```cpp
SetBackPropagate(kFALSE);
```

so the initial candidate construction uses the first fitted track parameters and does not force the track back to the origin.

The initial proton and antiproton candidates are then analyzed by:

- `macro/target/ana_dpm.C`

`ana_dpm.C` combines the proton and antiproton candidates and evaluates their geometric point of closest approach using:

```cpp
RhoVtxPoca::GetPocaVtx(...)
```

The resulting coordinates and distance of closest approach are stored as:

```text
proton_pbar_vtx_x
proton_pbar_vtx_y
proton_pbar_vtx_z
proton_pbar_doca
```

For the two-pass workflow, `ana_dpm.C` writes two complementary products:

- `<prefix>_boost.root`, containing an `event_poca` tree with exactly one entry per input event;
- `<prefix>_vtx_fit.json`, containing fitted sample-level means and widths for diagnostics and legacy fixed-IP compatibility.

The event-level tree stores:

```text
event_id
x
y
z
valid
```

The `valid` flag is set only when the event contains at least one proton and one antiproton candidate and the POCA result is finite.

### 3.3 First PID pass and POCA determination

The first PID pass is implemented by:

- `macro/target/pid_complete.C`

It configures `PndPidCorrelator` with:

```cpp
SetBackPropagate(kFALSE);
```

so the initial candidate construction uses the first fitted track parameters and does not force the track back to the origin.

The initial proton and antiproton candidates are then analyzed by:

- `macro/target/ana_dpm.C`

`ana_dpm.C` combines the proton and antiproton candidates and evaluates their geometric point of closest approach using:

```cpp
RhoVtxPoca::GetPocaVtx(...)
```

The resulting coordinates and distance of closest approach are stored as:

```text
proton_pbar_vtx_x
proton_pbar_vtx_y
proton_pbar_vtx_z
proton_pbar_doca
```

For the two-pass workflow, `ana_dpm.C` writes two complementary products:

- `<prefix>_boost.root`, containing an `event_poca` tree with exactly one entry per input event;
- `<prefix>_vtx_fit.json`, containing fitted sample-level means and widths for diagnostics and legacy fixed-IP compatibility.

The event-level tree stores:

```text
event_id
x
y
z
valid
```

The `valid` flag is set only when the event contains at least one proton and one antiproton candidate and the POCA result is finite.

# PandaRoot

This software is designed to the specific needs of the PANDA experiment. It is used to perform event generation, particle transport ("simulation"), detector digitisation and reconstruction, particle identification as well as event analysis.


### Installation
For **user installation** instructions please refer to [docs/Installation/Install_PandaRoot.md](docs/Installation/Install_PandaRoot.md)

If you do **development**, please follow the instructions in [docs/Installation/Install_Developers.md](docs/Installation/Install_Developers.md)

The installation at the **GSI cluster** Virgo is described in [docs/Installation/Install_GSI.md](docs/Installation/Install_GSI.md)

### Examples
To run a simulation chain with PandaRoot you can refer to `macro/master` which contains the most recent macros. More detailed examples and tutorials are found under `tutorials`. The most recent one is `tutorials/thailand2017`.

### Overview

There are many event generators, which can be found in `pgenerators`. The detector code is put at `detectors`. Under `geometry` the root geometries and related files are stored. 
The input and the parameters are located in `config`, `gconfig`, `input` and `macro/params`. Tracking and PID code is located in `tracking`, `genfit`, `genfit2` and `pid`. 
The analysis related classes are found in `analysis`. 
All data formats are separated from the actual algorithms and can be referenced in `pnddata`.

Under `macro/QA` you will find the quality assurance checks, which are performed each night. Their results can be found at [https://cdash.gsi.de/index.php?project=PandaRoot](https://cdash.gsi.de/index.php?project=PandaRoot).

4
LUMINOSITY DETERMINATION - THE LUMINOSITY FIT FRAMEWORK
This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. One possibility is to correct the measured data for the effects introduced by the ¯ PANDA spectrometer, which then allows a direct comparison with the pure elastic scattering model. Alternatively, the pure model can be modified to include all of the effects that arise during the measurement, so that is directly comparable with the data. The first option is in practice not feasible as required operations such as deconvolutions, which undo the detector resolution of the data, require very large amounts of data and a constant resolution to work reliably. On these grounds the second option was chosen, allowing for far more flexibility, extraction power and precision. The construction of the fit model with all of the transformations and correction procedures of the elastic scattering cross section is presented in detail in the following. Results on the extracted luminosity precision and studies of systematic uncertainties are presented in the next chapter.
4 . 1 the elastic scattering model
The cross section for elastic ¯ pp scattering was introduced in section 3 . 3 . Apart from the calculable coulomb part of the total elastic cross section, two possible parameterizations for the description of the hadronic part exist. Both parameterizations are implemented in the LuminosityFit software. Despite the fact that the E 760 parameterization is more suitable, because it uses more measurements in the four momentum range of the LMD, the DPM parameterization was chosen for the studies in this thesis (see equation 18 ). The reasoning is that the DPM generator is the only official generator for the ¯ PANDA experiment that includes elastic ¯ pp processes 1 . This chapter presents the LuminosityFit software, which counts as major work effort of this thesis, and can be found on the github platform [ 107 ]. It is responsible for the determination of the luminosity with the highest possible precision from the reconstructed data of the LMD. Recalling chapter 3 , this is achieved by comparing the measured elastic scattering angular distribution with the theoretical model distribution. The normalization variable is the absolute luminosity L . However the measured angular distribution N ( θ ) cannot simply be compared to the theoretical model σ ( θ ) , because several inevitable measurement effects alter the original pure elastic scattering distribution. There are two possible paths to overcome this obstacle. Figure 5.6: Modified Restgas profiles with ±10% density variations (orange and
green curves) compared to the nominal profile (blue curve).
The contrast between the consistent and mismatched scenarios leads to a critical
conclusion: The LuminosityFit framework is capable of high precision, but its ac-
curacy is strictly limited by the knowledge of the underlying longitudinal target
density profile 𝜌(𝑧).
A 3% systematic uncertainty induced by unnoticed Restgas variation is unaccept-
able. To mitigate this, one cannot rely on the LMD alone, as it cannot provide
the target profile including the Restgas background during data taking. Therefore,
an independent and precise measurement of the target and Restgas distribution is
required. This necessitates the use of the tracking systems in PANDA, particularly a
detector with high vertex resolution close to the interaction point.
This motivation leads directly to the next part of this thesis: the feasibility study
of using the tracking system of the PANDA Target Spectrometer in order to pre-
cisely measure the target density profile along the beam axis, including the Restgas
distribution.

[evidence.a38328afd315febbdd3a10e5, evidence.daf87fef8bd84f737d023fd8]
In data/PndLmdDataReader.cxx, inspect producer filtering and accounting: tracks are skipped if they fail reconstruction (wasReconstructed checking track_info.IsReconstructedAtIP for RECO or MC_ACC), if MC tracks are flagged as secondary (track_info.IsSecondary), or if track parameters fall outside ranges evaluated by successfullyPassedFilters; for acceptance objects, non-secondary tracks are recorded with track_accepted to tally accepted-versus-generated entries. [evidence.9b11380bf90f5bf9e8f0e312]
At the consumer stage in apps/runLmdFit.cxx, confirm that the input directory paths (-d for elastic data, -a for acceptance, and -r for reference acceptance) contain the matched regex filenames, and verify schema compatibility: runLmdFit filters data with DataPrimaryDimensionOptionsFilter targeting LumiFit::THETA_X and track_type MC, MC_ACC, or RECO (conditioned on fit.fit_model_options.acceptance_correction_active and resolution_smearing_active) plus NoSecondaryTrackFilter, which discards all data if prepared bundles have mismatched dimensions or active selections. [evidence.daf87fef8bd84f737d023fd8, evidence.deb73f9fcdc045419651d3a8]
When verifying acceptance and efficiency distributions, numerator-empty bins can stem from reconstruction selection cuts (such as IsReconstructedAtIP or recCut pvz != -999.0) and resolution migration, whereas bins with zero generated denominator counts yield undefined/zero efficiency and must be protected by denominator/efficiency checks (such as eff > 0) across consistent variable binning and profile ranges (nBinsVar, xBinsVar). [evidence.9b11380bf90f5bf9e8f0e312, evidence.ed959b5c98687ff96b42df06, evidence.4c8c16a447da23f89b4b8f0b]

[evidence.9b11380bf90f5bf9e8f0e312]
When diagnosing empty efficiency bins, evaluate both sides of the ratio: zero-count numerators occur when reconstructed tracks fail cuts (such as recCut pvz != -999.0) or migrate across bins due to resolution bias (tracked via pBias and hDev), while zero-count denominators in generated histograms (hMCGen == 0) create undefined efficiencies that must be handled by setting weights to zero and requiring eff > 0, ensuring consistent variable binning (nBinsVar, xBinsVar) across all reconstructed, generated, and profile histograms. Master Macros
=============

Introduction
------------

The master macros are the standard simulation and reconstruction macros of PandaRoot. 
They use the :ref:`MasterTasks` to have the most recent default settings for the detector simulation.

Running
-------

The typical sequence of macros is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- full_complete.C - Digitization, tracking and PID in one go
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

A sequence which expands the digi, reco and pid ito separate steps is:

- sim_complete.C - Event simulation. Set here the event generator you want to use
- digi_complete.C - Detector response simulation and local reconstruction
- reco_complete.C - Tracking
- pid_complete.C - Combine tracks with PID information
- ana_complete.C - Analysis of the data. Adopt here your analysis method

Common User Settings
--------------------

It is encouraged that you copy the macros to a location of your choice and work from there. 
For your own analysis you have to modify the ``sim_complete.C`` macro to set the proper event generation. EvtGen mostly serves for signal events, FTF for continuum background, while the BoxGenerator is there for detector studies.
Also you have to write your own analysis. 
The ``ana_complete.C`` macro may serve as a starting point. Also the tutorial section holds many examples to draw from.

The options available in the Master Tasks can be found at :ref:`MasterTasks`.

Typically the macro flow may look like this:

  nEvents=1000

# PandaRoot

This software is designed to the specific needs of the PANDA experiment. It is used to perform event generation, particle transport ("simulation"), detector digitisation and reconstruction, particle identification as well as event analysis.

Running Sequence
================

A complete PandaRoot simulation consists of several separated simulation stages.

.. image:: ../Images/PandaRootSimulationStages.png
  :width: 600
  :alt: Simulation stages in PandaRoot

Event Generator
---------------

First stage is the event generator. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.

Several different event generators exist for the different interaction scenarios.
For a more detailed description see :ref:`EventGenerators`.

Transport
-----------
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either `Geant3`_ or `Geant4`_
which can be seamlessly selected via `VMC`_.

In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields taken into account. It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.

.. _Geant3: https://vmc-project.github.io/user-guide/geant3+vmc/
.. _Geant4: https://geant4.web.cern.ch/
.. _VMC: https://vmc-project.github.io/

(Virtual Monte-Carlo [60]), ROOT (Plotting, ﬁtting, graphics etc. [61]), Pythia [62]
and auxiliary tools
• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

Running the software encloses a lot of algorithms and packages. A comprehensive overview is given in
Running Sequence
. For a quick way to set up everything it is recommended to familiarize with the
MasterTasks
. Developers also should have a look at the useful logging possibilities in
Using the Logger from Fair
.
Event Generation
¶
First stage is the event generation. It simulates the interaction of the antiproton beam with the target.
It does not include any interaction with the PANDA detector which is important for the decay of long living charged particles like hyperons.
Transport
¶
In the second stage the particles generated via the event generator are transported through the detector. This is done via either
Geant3
or
Geant4
which can be seamlessly selected via
VMC
.
In this stage the particle properties like their decay length, interaction with the detector material and fields are taken into account.
It creates a realistic picture about the processes taking place inside the detector. The output of this stage is
a Monte Carlo truth list of generated particles with their point of origin, momentum, charge and creation time, and, for each sub-detector, a list
of points where the particles have interacted with sensitive detector material, containing the time, position and lost energy at that point.
Digitization
¶
In the digitization stage the detector responds to the deposited charge in the sensitive volume is simulated.
In contains both the sensor properties as well as the readout electronics features of a subdetector.
The output should be a data stream matching with the one generated by the DAQ of the real PANDA experiment.
What is simulated and how detailed the simulation is, differs for each sub-detector.
Reconstruction
¶
The reconstruction is subdivided into two stages, the local reconstruction and the global reconstruction.
Local Reconstruction
¶
The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

and auxiliary tools
• FairRoot handling the framework (data I/O, interfaces, infrastructure). The task
is to provide all steps of the data processing up to the physics analysis stage.
Data is stored in a ROOT ﬁle, using ROOT objects handling with chains, trees and
branches.
• DetectorRoot detector framework (detector simulations and data reconstruction).
For the Panda experiment such framework is called PandaRoot.
The PandaRoot framework user should add detector class implementations for the
transport model and reconstruction tasks, which are processing the data. A typical chain
of generating and processing of simulated data contains the following ingredients:
1. Event Generator:
The event generator produces in each event a set of particles according to the in-
vestigated physics reaction or detector studies. Particles are deﬁned by their type
and four-momentum, point of origin and time. Those properties are randomly
distributed by the selected model. In PandaRoot for this purpose several gener-
ators are available. The "BOX" generator provides a uniform distribution for all
variables. It also has possibility to choose a certain variable range. A generator
for single-channel generation is called EvtGen [63]. And the DPM [64] generator
provides the full description of all antiproton-proton reactions.
2. Transport Code (VMC):
The particle transport through matter is simulated by Geant [58],[59]. The Virtual
Monte-Carlo interface (VMC) allows to switch between the diﬀerent Geant ver-
sions as well as to introduce other packages. Each sub-detector has its own geom-
etry description (usually in ROOT format) and deﬁnition of the active and passive
elements. For all materials in which particles can interact according to physical
processes, such as ionization, showering or Cherenkov emission, they react with
the detector material and loss of energy is estimated. Interaction of particle with
the detector material (e.g position and energy loss) is saved in each event. This
data is called MCHits and it is accessible for the analysis of the performance of
the reconstruction steps.
3. Digitization:
All Monte-Carlo data is processed to model the detectors response. The threshold,
eﬃciency and ampliﬁcation can be adjusted according to the measurements of
real detector response. The digitized data formats in the simulation must be the
same as those obtained in a real implementation (a prototype detector or even
the ﬁnal setup). This data is called DigiHits and is used as input information for
reconstruction of the events.

The local reconstruction is operating on the sub-detector data independently from each other and is part of the sub-detector code.
It translates the digitized detector data back into physical quantities like the translation from fired detector channel into a position in the detector,
or an ADC value back into an energy.
Global Reconstruction/Tracking
¶
Global reconstruction in PANDA mainly means reconstructing the track of charged particles from the measured hit points in the tracking detector.
This process happens again in two stages. The firs one is the track finding and pre-fitting stage. Here the hit points are sorted into
groups of hits which could belong to one track and a rough estimate of the track parameters like charge, momentum and position on track are calculated.
In the second stage a Kalman filter is used to improve the track parameters by taking also energy loss and multiple scattering into account
which is typically neglected in the pre-fitting stage.
Particle Identification
¶
The last stage before the analysis is the particle identification (PID). Here the tracks of the global reconstruction are combined with the measurements
of the PID detectors and the EMC and a probability for each stable particle species is calculated (e, pi, mu, K, p).
The complete information about one particle is then stored in a charged candidate. For those cluster in the EMC where no track is pointing to
an addition neutral candidate is created.
Analysis
¶
A analysis of a simulated physics channel or background data is performed using the Rho package.

records.question: How is beam-divergence smearing implemented in LuminosityFit?

result.answer:
In PndLmdModelFactory::generate2DModel within model/PndLmdModelFactory.cxx, when divergence_smearing_active is set in the configuration and data dimensions match LumiFit::THETA_X and LumiFit::THETA_Y, beam-divergence smearing is configured by instantiating a 2D Gaussian divergence model (GaussianModel2D) and constructing a PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D with it and the angular grid dimensions. [evidence.08873b527eb593d445b58bdf]
In the same factory method, the smearing component is incorporated into the fit model by wrapping the current CachedModel2D with a PndLmdDifferentialSmearingConvolutionModel2D that takes the PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D instance and injects the Gaussian divergence parameters gauss_sigma_var1 and gauss_sigma_var2 into the resulting model. [evidence.08873b527eb593d445b58bdf]
Inside model/PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D.cxx, PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D generates the divergence smearing map by discretizing the 2D domain according to data bin sizes and integrating the underlying Gaussian model across each 2D bin range to assemble smearing weights stored as DifferentialCoordinateContribution records. [evidence.5eafe820c8a090563c8abb46, evidence.06cd4db51bd9fa35aa1e4c06]

5 . 2 . 4 Accelerator Beam Divergence
In analogy to the distribution of the interaction point, the accelerator beam particles are distributed around the mean tilt. This distribution is also known as the beam divergence. Similar to the tilt, the beam divergence will also directly influence the elastic cross section. More precisely, the physics coordinate system is now no longer the same for the individual beam particles, as it has to be aligned to the flight direction. Because the physics scattering process is independent on the orientation of the coordinate system, the beam divergence is identical to a smearing of the elastic cross section by the divergence distribution in the reference frame aligned to the mean beam tilt.
Again the influence of the beam divergence on the accuracy of the luminosity determination can be studied by generating data samples from simulations with various divergences, while assuming no divergence when performing the luminosity fit. For the parameterization of the divergence a two dimensional normal distribution was chosen, as this is to be expected. Additional insight about the parameterization of the divergence can later be gained from beam measurements by the HESR group. Three different values for the standard deviation of the distributions div x , y = 0 . 1 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 35 mrad , independently in the θ x and θ y dimension, were simulated.

Here the div ( θ lab x , θ lab y , θ lab x ′ , θ lab y ′ ) is the function for the beam divergence that depends on not only the initial space parameters θ lab x ′ , θ lab y ′ , but also the final ones θ lab x , θ lab y . The θ lab x ′ , θ lab y ′ variables are being integrated over. Usually the divergence can be expressed with the differences of the variables from the primed and unprimed coordinate system and the divergence changes to div ( θ lab x -θ lab x ′ , θ lab y -θ lab y ′ ) , then the operation is more commonly referred to as the convolution. This description in terms of differences is of course only valid as long as the divergence has this symmetry. For a more thorough discussion of this topic see appendix B. 4 . Luckily this is very often the case, and specifically for the LMD a 2 D normal distribution is used for the divergence function. All parameters of the model are absorbed by the vector # α = ( tilt x , tilt y , div x , div y ) .
On the one hand the divergence gives the angular distribution of the antiproton beam particles around its mean tilt. This means that the physics coordinate system is different for each individual scattering event, as it is defined by the direction of flight of the initial state. However, because the scattering process is invariant under rotations 4 , the beam divergence is identical to a smearing of the elastic cross section by the divergence distribution. Therefore it can also be interpreted as the probability density function for a particle, which is initially within the angular element in the direction θ lab x ′ , θ lab y ′ , to wind up in the neighboring direction θ lab x , θ lab y .
4 Invariant under rotations means that the scattering process can be rotated as a whole and the physics outcome is not altered by this transformation.

A Beam Tilt is defined by two small angles: 𝑡 𝑥 (tilt in the 𝑥 -𝑧 plane) and 𝑡 𝑦 (tilt in the 𝑦 -𝑧 plane). A non-zero tilt introduces a systematic shift in the scattering angles, the relationship between the true scattering angle 𝜃 * and the angle 𝜃 𝑙𝑎𝑏 measured in the detector frame is approximated by:

Neglecting this tilt induces a spurious 𝜑 -dependence in the data. The measured polar angle 𝜃 𝑙𝑎𝑏 would be systematically shifted depending on 𝜑 , distorting the 𝑡 -distribution and ruining the fit quality. The LuminosityFit framework treats the Beam Tilt as a coordinate transformation. The reconstructed momentum vectors of all tracks are rotated from the 'Laboratory Frame' into the 'Beam Reference Frame' using a rotation matrix 𝑅 ( 𝑡 𝑥 , 𝑡 𝑦 ), effectively aligning the effective beam axis with the 𝑧 -axis for the analysis, which define the variables 𝜃 𝑥 and 𝜃 𝑦 :
Beam Divergence
In contrast to the coherent tilt, the Beam Divergence represents the intrinsic statistical spread of the particle directions within the beam bunch. It follows a Gaussian distribution with width 𝜎 𝑑𝑖𝑣 . Since the initial direction of a specific antiproton is unknown, this effect cannot be corrected event-by-event. Instead, it acts as an irreducible angular smearing.
In the luminosity fit model, the beam divergence is treated by convolution. It adds in quadrature to the detector's intrinsic resolution 𝑅 𝑑𝑒𝑡 . The total effective resolution kernel 𝑅 𝑒𝑓𝑓 is given by:
where 𝐺 denotes the normalized Gaussian distribution describing the beam divergence:
Here, the mean 𝜇 = 0 reflects the fact that the systematic mean direction (Tilt) has already been corrected, leaving only the stochastic spread 𝜎 = 𝜎 𝑑𝑖𝑣 to be convolved. While the transverse width is handled in the Acceptance (multiplicative term), the divergence is handled in the Resolution (convolution kernel), ensuring a mathematically consistent treatment of all beam properties.
3.7 Integrated Fit Workflow
To rigorously account for the beam properties discussed above, the luminosity determination follows a sequential five-step workflow as illustrated in Figure 3.11. This procedure ensures that the physics model used for the fit matches the specific experimental conditions of the data taking period.

result.answer:
In model/PndLmdModelFactory.cxx, when divergence_smearing_active is configured for 2D angular data in THETA_X and THETA_Y coordinates, PndLmdModelFactory::generate2DModel constructs a GaussianModel2D instance and passes it along with the angular dimension specifications to instantiate a PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D object. [evidence.08873b527eb593d445b58bdf, evidence.06cd4db51bd9fa35aa1e4c06]
In model/PndLmdModelFactory.cxx, PndLmdModelFactory::generate2DModel integrates divergence smearing into the fit model by constructing a PndLmdDifferentialSmearingConvolutionModel2D that wraps the cached differential cross-section model and the PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D, subsequently injecting the divergence Gaussian parameters gauss_sigma_var1 and gauss_sigma_var2 into the resulting convolution model. [evidence.08873b527eb593d445b58bdf]
In model/PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D.cxx, PndLmdDivergenceSmearingModel2D discretizes the divergence model across a two-dimensional grid matching the data bin sizes and computes smearing probabilities via multi-threaded numerical integration using IntegralStrategyGSL2D, storing them as a list of DifferentialCoordinateContribution objects. [evidence.5eafe820c8a090563c8abb46, evidence.a8393fe1badc6e8a71322f45, evidence.5a4652908bf6aa8e9fb96aaf]
In PndLmdModelFactory::generateModel, the factory receives the configuration property tree model_opt_ptree and the input PndLmdAngularData, branches on fit_dimension to invoke generate2DModel, and returns the assembled fit Model that incorporates the divergence smearing convolution layer. [evidence.08873b527eb593d445b58bdf]

records.question: Why is restgas longitudinal reconstruction efficiency profile dependent?

result.answer:
Restgas longitudinal reconstruction efficiency is profile dependent because the central target density (around z ≈ ±1 cm) is approximately 10^2 times higher than the surrounding restgas background, causing finite detector spatial resolution smearing to produce a large net asymmetric migration ('spill-over') of reconstructed target events into adjacent restgas longitudinal bins. [evidence.1153088011fdad613d84d4cd]
A uniform density MC profile yields symmetric migration where events smearing in and out balance, resulting in an efficiency bounded at or below 100% that fails to model the real data net migration artifact and would misinterpret target spill-over events as genuine restgas, grossly overestimating the gas density near the interaction point. [evidence.1153088011fdad613d84d4cd]
To compensate for resolution smearing without ill-posed deconvolution, a forward-modeling approach generates simulation events using a realistic input density profile rho_in(z) (set via restgas_profile in prod_sim_hvmaps.C) and defines the reconstructed-coordinate efficiency as epsilon_reco,i = N_MC,rec(z_reco in i) / N_MC,gen(z_true in i), which incorporates both geometrical acceptance and target-to-restgas migration so that dividing raw data by epsilon_reco mathematically cancels the migration present in the measured numerator. [evidence.1153088011fdad613d84d4cd, evidence.473633c6eb40ed4e9438a436, evidence.ea00f0b85a4689932e927f9d, evidence.ed959b5c98687ff96b42df06]

Determination of the Restgas Profile
8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

Determination of the Restgas Profile
8.2 Resolution Effects and Profile-Dependent Efficiency
A more subtle yet critical challenge in the efficiency correction arises from the finite spatial resolution of the detector, particularly at the interface between the target and the Restgas background. The particle density of the target in the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ≈ ± 1 cm) is approximately 10 2 times higher than that of the surrounding Restgas background. This extreme density contrast, coupled with the stochastic vertex smearing, necessitates a correction strategy that goes beyond simple geometrical acceptance.
To quantify this effect, an efficiency map was generated using a realistic Monte Carlo simulation, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input model. The resulting efficiency curve (shown as the orange curve in Figure 8.1) differs fundamentally from the one derived using a standard uniform density profile ( 𝜌 𝑀𝐶 = const, shown as the green curve). A specific feature in the realistic profile-dependent map highlights the impact of spatial resolution smearing. In the transition region immediately adjacent to the target ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -10 . 0 , +10 . 0] cm), the calculated efficiency 𝜖 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 forms distinct peaks that drastically exceed unity ( 𝜖 > 100%). This anomaly is a direct manifestation of the 'spill-over' effect: due to resolution smearing, the massive migration of events out of the high-density target bins significantly outnumbers the genuine Restgas events generated in those adjacent locations. In contrast, a uniform MC distribution yields a smooth, bounded efficiency curve ( 𝜖 𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑓𝑜𝑟𝑚 ≤ 1) that severely underestimates the true efficiency in this critical transition region. In such a uniform scenario, the migration of events is inherently symmetric-the number of events smearing into a specific bin is roughly balanced by those smearing out. Consequently, applying a uniform efficiency map completely fails to capture the net migration artifact present in the real data. Doing so would incorrectly interpret the target 'spill-over' events as a genuine Restgas signal, ultimately leading to a gross overestimation of the actual gas density near the interaction point.
To address this resolution smearing, mathematically deconvolving the detector resolution from the measured data would in principle be possible. However, deconvolution is notoriously sensitive to noise and often becomes mathematically ill-posed, especially in low-statistics regions. Therefore, a 'forward modeling' approach is adopted. Instead of attempting to remove the resolution from the data, the resolution effects are incorporated directly into the efficiency correction. Monte Carlo samples are generated using a realistic input density profile, 𝜌 𝑖𝑛 ( 𝑧 ), which includes the high-density target peak and mimics the true physics distribution. As a result, the reconstructed events 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 naturally reproduce the same resolution smearing and target-to-Restgas migration observed in the experimental data, while the generated MC events 𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 represent the underlying truth information. The efficiency is defined as the ratio of reconstructed to generated MC events 𝜀 = 𝑁 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 /𝑁 𝑔𝑒𝑛 , effectively acting as a convolved correction function that encapsulates both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration. When this specific efficiency map is applied to the experimental data, the resolution effects present in the numerator are mathematically cancelled by those modeled in the efficiency, enabling the recovery of the true underlying Restgas profile without the numerical instabilities associated with deconvolution.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

The intrinsic consistency of the method was first verified under ideal conditions where the input profile used for efficiency generation matches the true physical distribution. This baseline scenario serves as a sanity check to confirm that the method can accurately recover the Restgas profile when the model is correct. Figure 8.2 presents the comparison between the reconstructed Restgas profile and the initial truth distribution over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. This result represents the ideal control scenario where the input distribution used to generate the efficiency map is identical to the true physical distribution. To accommodate the large density gradients, the vertical axis is plotted in logarithmic scale. Additionally, the inset provides a zoomed view of the central interaction region ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -30 , +30]cm) to visualize the reconstruction quality in the high-density zone. The reconstructed results exhibit excellent agreement with the true distribution across the entire longitudinal range. In the critical central region ( 𝑧 ∈ [ -30 , +30]cm), the method achieves a high precision with a loss of events during reconstruction of -0 . 24 ± 0 . 29%. In the extended upstream and downstream regions, slightly larger fluctuations are observed due to the reduced statistics and lower detection efficiency. However, these deviations remain within acceptable limits. For the full range covering 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m, the 1 . 16 ± 1 . 27% more events are reconstructed. This result confirms that the profiledependent efficiency correction successfully recovers the integrated Restgas density and shape over the full experimental domain.

A precise track reconstruction in the LMD relies on a precise knowledge of the IP, which
is used as the destination point for the back propagation. In simulation studies, the IP
is known with inﬁnite precision, which will not be the case later in the experiment. One
should consider the following eﬀects:

2. Target spatial distribution
3. Beam shift and tilt
4. Target shift and tilt
5. Rest gas
The rest gas can be considered as an extreme limit of target and the beam shifts, where
the IP is signiﬁcantly shifted to large values along the x, y and z axis. The expected
amount of the rest gas is rather high and ∼10% of the target material can be expected
in the narrow beam pipe around the IP [78].
With the current track reconstruction, we can determine only a systematic shift of
the IP. One can use the ﬂexibility of the back propagation procedure during which the
track is recalculated to the PCA of the IP. In case of a systematic shift of the IP, this is
visible by the mean values of the PCA distribution for a bunch of reconstructed tracks.
To study the accuracy of reconstruction of the shifted IP, 106 tracks with a momen-

within 2 and 12mrad and φMC from 0 to 2π. For the beam a Gaussian shape with

with a Gaussian shape with 0.08cm widths. And again the z coordinate of the IP was
simulated uniformly within −50 to 50cm. This emulates situation when interaction
happens with the rest gas in the beam pipe near the IP.

support_spans: Why is restgas longitudinal reconstruction efficiency profile dependent?

claims.claim_text: The restgas longitudinal reconstruction efficiency is profile dependent because finite detector spatial resolution smearing couples with an extreme density contrast—where target density in the central interaction region (z ≈ ±1 cm) is roughly 10^2 times higher than the surrounding restgas background—causing massive net migration ('spill-over') of reconstructed events from the high-density target bins into adjacent restgas bins.

Because the reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is defined as ε_reco,i = N_MC,rec(z_reco ∈ i) / N_MC,gen(z_true ∈ i), the numerator records reconstructed coordinates that embed both geometrical acceptance and resolution-induced migration; unlike a uniform density profile where bin migration is symmetrically balanced, steep physical density gradients cause net migration that directly changes the local efficiency ratio (even exceeding 100% in transition regions like z ∈ [-10.0, +10.0] cm).

Under the forward-modeling approach used to avoid numerical instabilities from deconvolution, the efficiency map must be generated using an input density profile ρ_in(z) that mimics the physical target and restgas distribution so that the modeled target-to-restgas migration in the efficiency numerator mathematically cancels the net migration artifact present in the measured experimental data.

response.reason: All claims are strictly supported by the cited thesis and documentation excerpts. They accurately explain why the restgas longitudinal reconstruction efficiency depends on the profile: finite spatial resolution smearing combined with steep density contrast causes net migration into adjacent bins, altering the reconstructed-coordinate efficiency ratio, which requires realistic forward modeling to cancel out the migration artifact. The answer requirement applies only to composition or factory questions, so it is not omitted here.

claims.claim_text: To construct the simulation sample reflecting the profile dependence for efficiency calculation, the input profile is configured in the PndMasterRunSim simulation manager via setters such as SetTargetMode(8) and SetRestGasProfile(restgas_profile) alongside generator and beam configuration, followed by construction through Setup(), module and geometry building, AddSimTasks(), Init(), and Run(nEvents) to produce the simulated MC events.

Chapter9 Summary of the Luminosity
Determination
The capability of the PANDA detector, specifically the upgraded Micro Vertex Detector (MVD) utilizing HVMAPS technology has been established, to perform a precise, data-driven measurement of the Restgas density profile over the full range of 𝑧 ∈ [ -3 . 0 , +6 . 0] m. The superior vertexing resolution and reduced material budget of the sensors are critical factors that enable the effective determination of the Restgas distribution even for interactions significantly displaced from the nominal IP.
Through the implementation of a profile-dependent efficiency correction and a robust iterative workflow, the systematic distortions caused by resolution smearing and initial model inaccuracies are rigorously suppressed. This method acts as a contracting map, converging to the true physical distribution and ensuring that the final result is independent of the initial simulation input provided by the Target Group. To quantify the stability of this approach, an iterative procedure was initialized with an extreme starting condition: a 40% overestimation of the Restgas distribution. As summarized in Table 9.1, the iterative procedure converges rapidly. Within merely three steps, the global deviation drops from 12 . 27% to 1 . 30%, and the deviation in the central region vanishes to -0 . 22%. Consequently, the precise density profile can be derived directly from the experimental data across the entire relevant domain, providing the reliable input essential for the absolute luminosity determination.
Finally, the determined Restgas profile was integrated back into the LuminosityFit framework to validate the complete analysis chain. The luminosity determination was performed at a beam momentum of 𝑝 𝑏𝑒𝑎𝑚 = 4 . 06 GeV /𝑐 , applying a cut within the analysis window ( | 𝑥 | , | 𝑦 | < 1 cm and | 𝑧 | < 5 cm). The relative deviation of the determined luminosity (Δ ℒ / ℒ ) is (0 . 05 ± 0 . 07)% with the reconstructed target profile with Restgas background. As presented in Table 9.2, this result is consistent with the ideal case where the target is treated as point-like and the efficiency correction is based on a point-like model, which yields a deviation of -0 . 036 ± 0 . 07% and also with the case where the target profile with Restgas background is well-known and totally the same as real data, which yields a deviation of 0 . 02 ± 0 . 08%. This results demonstrate that the synergy of high-precision tracking and advanced fitting algorithms transforms the Restgas background from a limiting systematic background into a precisely monitored observable, enabling a robust and accurate luminosity determination for the PANDA experiment.

Outside the central region, the fluctuations are slightly larger due to lower statistics but remain within acceptable limits. Even when the deviation exceeds 10%, the magnitude of the deviation is significantly smaller than the initial input bias, demonstrating that the measurement process acts as a contracting map. Based on these observations, a robust iterative workflow is established for the application to real experimental data:
Initialization: The initial efficiency map is derived from a simulation of approximately 5 × 10 6 events using the DPM generator, taking the density profile provided by the Target Group as the input distribution.
Reconstruction: The experimental data is reconstructed using this efficiency map.
Convergence Check: The resulting reconstructed profile 𝜌 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 is compared with the input profile 𝜌 𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡 used for the efficiency correction. Iteration: If the deviation exceeds the threshold, the reconstructed profile 𝜌 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜 is adopted as the new input model to generate an updated efficiency map. The process (Steps 2-3) is repeated until the convergence criterion is met.

Check with the Ideal Case
135
This choice, however, introduces a potential logical paradox: the generation of the correct efficiency map seems to require prior knowledge of the very Restgas distribution to be measured. This creates a circular dependency, as the input profile must be known before the measurement can be performed. In practice, this circularity is resolved by treating the measurement as an iterative process. The nominal Restgas profile provided by the Target Group, which is based on vacuum simulations and nozzle geometry, serves as the initial estimator. While this theoretical prediction may contain uncertainties regarding the absolute density or the precise shape, it provides a sufficient topological baseline to model the resolution migration. The strength of the method lies in its ability to refine this initial guess: the PANDA detector's high-precision tracking provides experimental feedback that is significantly more sensitive than the initial model.
Therefore, the critical question is not whether the initial input is perfect, but rather whether the method is robust against imperfections in the input. It must be verified if a distorted initial profile leads to a biased final measurement, or if the method converges to the true physical distribution regardless of the starting point.

8.3 Check with the Ideal Case
To validate the stability of the efficiency correction and to address the circular dependency issue, systematic studies were performed. The core objective was to quantify the sensitivity of the final measurement to inaccuracies in the initial input model. This was achieved by intentionally introducing discrepancies between the 'true' physical distribution (used to generate the pseudo-data) and the 'input' model (used to generate the efficiency map).

### 3.7 Iterative removal of input-profile dependence

The efficiency depends weakly on the profile used in the MC because resolution migration is profile dependent. This appears to create a circular problem: the profile is needed to calculate the efficiency used to measure the profile.

The intended solution is iterative:

1. Start from the nominal Target Group profile $\rho_0(z)$.
2. Generate MC and calculate $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},0}(z)$.
3. Correct the measured spectrum to obtain $\rho_1(z)$.
4. Use $\rho_1(z)$ as the next MC input.
5. Repeat until the profile or integrated correction changes negligibly.

The thesis robustness study tests mismatches between the “true” pseudo-data profile and the profile used for the efficiency MC. The method substantially reduces the initial model bias, especially in the central high-statistics region.

### 3.6 Profile-dependent efficiency correction

The raw reconstructed spectrum is related to the true profile through acceptance, selection efficiency, and resolution migration.

A simple “truth-coordinate” efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{truth},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

For Restgas determination, the more useful profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate efficiency is

```math
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{MC,rec}}(z_{\mathrm{reco}}\in i)}
     {N_{\mathrm{MC,gen}}(z_{\mathrm{true}}\in i)}.
```

Because its numerator is filled in reconstructed coordinates, this map includes both geometrical efficiency and migration caused by finite vertex resolution. The corrected profile is then estimated bin-by-bin as

```math
N_{\mathrm{corr},i}
=
\frac{N_{\mathrm{data,rec},i}}
     {\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reco},i}}.
```

This is a forward-model correction rather than an explicit deconvolution. If the MC input profile resembles the physical profile sufficiently well, the migration present in the measured numerator is compensated by the migration encoded in the efficiency map.

The main correction code is located in:

- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_1.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_2.C`
- `macro/target/correction/efficiency_correction_steps.C`
- `macro/target/correction/run_efficiency_batch.py`

Recommended interpretation:

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `efficiency_correction.C` | Central-region diagnostic, default range $[-30,+30]$ cm |
| `efficiency_correction_1.C` | Earlier wide-range version |
| `efficiency_correction_2.C` | Current wide-range analysis used by `run_efficiency_batch.py`; supports file-index ranges and non-uniform binning |
| `efficiency_correction_steps.C` | Method/debug study with explicit intermediate steps |
| `run_efficiency_batch.py` | Runs the true-profile versus input-profile robustness matrix |

`efficiency_correction_2.C` calculates both `hEff` and `hEffReco`. The histogram

```text
hCorrected_RecoEff
```

is the direct implementation of the profile-dependent reconstructed-coordinate correction above.

The macro also contains a **hybrid analysis variant**:

- in the current `efficiency_correction_2.C`, use truth-coordinate efficiency for $-2 \le z \le 2$ cm;
- use reconstructed-coordinate efficiency outside this central interval.

Earlier correction variants use slightly different central boundaries, so the numerical cut should be checked in the selected macro before comparing results. This hybrid definition is an analysis choice and should not be confused with the general correction formula.

The correction macros use English comments and plotting annotations; these presentation changes do not alter the numerical correction logic.

Cluster-jet target
A disadvantage of a pellet target is the variation of the luminosity with the pellet ﬂux.
In this respect, clearly, a cluster-jet target with a homogeneous distribution of hydrogen
atoms in the antiproton beam is better. The cluster-jet beam for the internal target in
the HESR is produced by expansion of pre-cooled gas in a convergent-divergent Laval-
type nozzle with micron-sized throat into vacuum. While passing through the nozzle,
the gas adiabatically cools down and forms a supersonic stream of atoms or molecules.
Under appropriate conditions, depending on the type of gas, condensation can take
place and nano-particles, the so-called clusters, are created. The size of such clusters
is strongly inﬂuenced by the experimental conditions such as the pressure and the
temperature of the gas before entering the nozzle. Furthermore, the throat diameter
and the shape of the supersonic part of the nozzle inﬂuences both the size of these
particles and the total cluster yield. Cluster beams can travel over several meters of
distance in a vacuum without changing their direction or shape. Also they have high
densities.
The density achieved so far is below that of a pellet target, however, the expecta-
tions in current R&D are that the luminosity requirements for PANDA can be fulﬁlled.
An additional advantage of a cluster-jet target is its homogeneous density proﬁle. Thus,
it is possible to focus the antiproton beam at highest phase-space density [30].
Both targets are connected to their source above the PANDA detector and to a dump

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Module to call the runLmdFit binary from an experiment config.

Can either be run as script with the experiment config as argument, or imported as module.
"""

import json

from lumifit.cluster import Job, JobResourceRequest
from lumifit.paths import generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath
from lumifit.types import ExperimentParameters


def createLumiFitJob(experiment: ExperimentParameters) -> Job:
    # allocate two times this many cores on a compute node, or we'll get a segfault.
    # 16 seems to work when we allocate 32 cores, so just leave it like that. the fit
    # only takes like five minutes anyway
    number_of_threads: int = 16

    LMDscriptpath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitScripts
    LMDbinPath = experiment.softwarePaths.LmdFitBuildDir
    elasticMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.dataPackage)
    resAccMergeDataPath = generateAbsoluteMergeDataPath(experiment.resAccPackage)
    config_url = experiment.fitConfigPath
    lumiFileName = experiment.lumiFileName

    resource_request = JobResourceRequest(walltime_in_minutes=12 * 60)
    resource_request.number_of_nodes = 1
    resource_request.processors_per_node = number_of_threads
    resource_request.memory_in_mb = 2000

    # use either the reconstructed IP or the IP from the experiment config
    # (data package reco settings)
    # this is slightly hacky, but the runLmdFit binary can't read the experiment config.
    # so we're reading the experiment config ourselves and write a second recoIP.json file
    # that we're passing

    if experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.use_ip_determination:
        recoIPfile = experiment.recoIPpath
    else:
        recoIPfile = experiment.experimentDir / "recoIP-fromConfig.json"
        with open(recoIPfile, "w") as f:
            externalIPjson = {
                "ip_x": experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.recoIPX,
                "ip_y": experiment.dataPackage.recoParams.recoIPY,
            }
            json.dump(externalIPjson, f)

    job = Job(
        resource_request,
        application_url=f"{LMDscriptpath}/singularityJob.sh '{LMDbinPath}/bin/runLmdFit -c {config_url} -d {elasticMergeDataPath} -a {resAccMergeDataPath} -m {number_of_threads} -o {lumiFileName} -i {recoIPfile}'",
        name="runLmdFit",
        logfile_url=str(elasticMergeDataPath / "runLmdFit.log"),
        array_indices=[1],
    )
    return job


if __name__ == "__main__":
    """
    Script part of this module. Just supply the experiment config file as argument.
    """
    import argparse
    from pathlib import Path

    from lumifit.cluster import ClusterJobManager
    from lumifit.config import load_params_from_file
    from lumifit.gsi_virgo import create_virgo_job_handler
    from lumifit.himster import create_himster_job_handler
    from lumifit.types import ClusterEnvironment, ExperimentParameters

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Script for going through whole directory trees and looking for bunches directories with filelists in them creating lmd data objects.",
        formatter_class=argparse.RawTextHelpFormatter,
    )

    parser.add_argument(
        "-e",
        "--experiment_config",
        dest="ExperimentConfigFile",
        type=Path,
        help="The Experiment.config file that holds all info.",
        required=True,
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    # load experiment config
    experiment: ExperimentParameters = load_params_from_file(args.ExperimentConfigFile, ExperimentParameters)

    lumiFitJob = createLumiFitJob(experiment)

    if experiment.cluster == ClusterEnvironment.VIRGO:
        job_handler = create_virgo_job_handler("long")
    elif experiment.cluster == ClusterEnvironment.HIMSTER:
        job_handler = create_himster_job_handler("himster2_exp")
    else:
        raise NotImplementedError(f"Cluster type {experiment.cluster} is not implemented!")

    # job threshold of this type (too many jobs could generate to much io load
    # as quite a lot of data is read in from the storage...)
    job_manager = ClusterJobManager(job_handler, total_job_threshold=2500)

    # for job in joblist:
    job_manager.enqueue(lumiFitJob)

    print("Job submitted!")
